name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# Cancel superseded runs on the same ref to save minutes.
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The db/server tests run against a real Postgres. global-setup.ts connects to
    # localhost:48802 (user/password hub) and creates a fresh hub_test database.
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:18
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: hub
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: hub
        ports:
          - 48802:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U hub"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 3s
          --health-retries 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@0ebf47130e4866e96fce0953f49152a61190b271 # v6.0.9
      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      # BUILD FIRST. This used to run after `pnpm test`, and the cli suite runs the built
      # `dist/index.js` rather than the sources - so the tests were asserting against
      # whatever dist happened to be lying around, never against the code in the commit.
      # 0.6.1 shipped a CLI that threw at import (two `program.command("channel")`
      # registrations, which commander rejects) with 185 cli tests green: tsc does not
      # see a runtime registration clash, tsup happily built it, and the suite ran an
      # older dist that predated the clash. Nothing was wrong with any single step; the
      # ORDER meant the thing under test was never the thing being shipped.
      - name: Build publishable CLI
        run: pnpm --filter @relayroom/cli build
      - name: Test
        run: pnpm test

  # What this job catches that `test` cannot: things MISSING FROM THE DOCKER BUILD
  # CONTEXT. `tsc --noEmit` and `pnpm build` run against the whole working tree, so a
  # file that exists in the repo but is never COPYed into the image looks fine to
  # both of them - and the image build is the only place that difference shows up.
  #
  # This is not hypothetical. 0.4.1 shipped with both web images failing to build:
  # apps/web/vitest.config.ts had started importing the shared test database URL
  # from test/, which the web Dockerfile did not copy, and `next build` type-checks
  # config files. Tests were green, `pnpm build` was green, and the break surfaced
  # only when someone pressed release - after npm had already published.
  #
  # amd64 only: this class of failure (missing context, type errors, missing deps,
  # Dockerfile syntax) is architecture-independent, and release-images.yml still
  # builds arm64 before anything is published. Two nets; no reason to make the first
  # one twice as heavy.
  #
  # push: false - nothing is published from here. A PR job that pushed would need
  # `packages: write`, and a fork PR's GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only, so pushing would
  # turn every outside contribution red. Building is the whole check.
  #
  # No path filter on purpose. The build context is the repo root, so almost any
  # file can change the result - the 0.4.1 break came from test/, which an
  # apps/**-and-packages/** filter would have skipped straight past. A filter that
  # is wrong disables this check silently, and it would be saving free runner
  # minutes on a public repo.
  images:
    name: Image build (docker context check)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        app: [server, web]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@d7f5e7f509e45cec5c76c4d5afdd7de93d0b3df5 # v4.1.0
      - name: Build ${{ matrix.app }} image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@f9f3042f7e2789586610d6e8b85c8f03e5195baf # v7.2.0
        with:
          context: .
          file: apps/${{ matrix.app }}/Dockerfile
          platforms: linux/amd64
          push: false
          # Scoped per app so the two matrix legs do not evict each other. mode=min
          # (final layers only) to stay small: the GHA cache is 10GB per repo with
          # LRU eviction, and crowding out setup-node's pnpm cache would cost the
          # `test` job more time than this job saves. Raise to max if builds are slow.
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=image-${{ matrix.app }}
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=min,scope=image-${{ matrix.app }}

# @relayroom/install

Interactive installer for self-hosting [RelayRoom](https://relayroom.dev).

```bash
npx @relayroom/install
```

It asks a few questions (install directory, public URLs, ports, optional SMTP),
generates strong secrets, and writes a self-contained `docker-compose.yml` + `.env`
that run the prebuilt public images from GHCR. No source checkout, no build step.
Optionally it can start the stack for you.

The pinned image version defaults to the installer's own version, so
`npx @relayroom/install@0.3.0` installs RelayRoom 0.3.0 - server and web move in
lockstep.

After it finishes:

```bash
cd relayroom
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 storage   # the container runs as uid 1000
docker compose up -d
```

Then open the dashboard URL and create the first admin account. The server runs
database migrations on boot, so there is nothing else to set up.

Run non-interactively (accept all defaults) with `-y`.

## Upgrading

`docker compose pull` only updates the images, never the `docker-compose.yml` you
already have - so compose-level changes in a new release would be missed. From your
install directory:

```bash
npx @relayroom/install@latest upgrade
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
```

`upgrade` regenerates `docker-compose.yml` and pins `RELAYROOM_VERSION` in `.env` to
the installer's version, keeping all your other `.env` values (secrets, URLs, SMTP).

Docs: https://relayroom.dev/docs
